text: An operating system update. On the cluster ARN the action is `os-upgrade`: it updates the operating systems of all DB instances in the cluster with rolling upgrades. On an instance ARN the action is `system-update`: it updates the operating system of that one instance; AWS keeps it for backward compatibility and recommends the cluster-level action. The description tells the two kinds apart: "New Operating System upgrade is available" is a move to a new Amazon Linux major version and is mandatory; "New Operating System patch is available" is a patch.

This cannot be expressed in code. The Terraform `aws_rds_cluster` and `aws_rds_cluster_instance`, CloudFormation `AWS::RDS::DBCluster` and CDK resources have a maintenance window, auto minor version upgrade and an engine version, and no argument that applies a pending maintenance action. No code change is needed and none causes drift.
AWS publishes no CVE list for this action: it returns the action, its dates and a generic description.

The cluster-level `os-upgrade` preserves read availability: Aurora updates a few reader instances at a time and the writer last, so there is one writer failover. Zero-downtime patching does not apply to operating system patches and upgrades. With the instance-level action, update the readers first and the writer last; each instance restarts in its own maintenance window.

An action with an apply date is applied by AWS in the maintenance window after that date (cluster-level updates use the cluster's window, instance-level ones each instance's window). Operating system distribution upgrades are mandatory. An action without a date is not applied automatically.

The person running this needs `rds:DescribePendingMaintenanceActions`, `rds:ApplyPendingMaintenanceAction`, `rds:DescribeDBClusters`, `rds:DescribeDBInstances`, `rds:DescribeEvents` and `rds:CreateDBClusterSnapshot` on this cluster and its instances.
Confirm what is pending on the cluster and on each instance, and read the dates.
Read which instance is the writer and that the cluster is `available`. If the cluster-level `os-upgrade` is offered, use it instead of patching instances one by one.
An `immediate` opt-in can't be undone. Take a manual cluster snapshot first so there is a known restore point.
RDS console, Region {region} > Databases > select `{id}` > Actions > Patch at next window (or Patch now). Defer upgrade stays available until the update starts.
Schedule it for the next maintenance window. Run it once per ARN listed under Scope, readers before the writer when the action is instance-level.
Or apply it now, in a quiet period. An immediate opt-in can't be undone.

The action leaves the pending list once applied. The list is eventually consistent: poll with backoff, starting at a couple of seconds, for up to five minutes. Then check every instance is `available` and the application reconnected after the writer failover.

A scheduled update that has not started can be cancelled with `undo-opt-in`. Once it has started it can't be deferred, and an immediate opt-in can't be undone. AWS documents no way to remove an applied operating system update.

An Aurora PostgreSQL engine patch. On a cluster ARN `system-update` means "patch the DB engine for Aurora PostgreSQL" (AWS's example description: "Upgrade to Aurora PostgreSQL 3.3.2"). The same action name on an instance ARN means an operating system update.

This cannot be expressed in code. The Aurora PostgreSQL engine version in the API, and so in Terraform, CloudFormation and CDK, is major.minor (for example `16.4`). The patch is a third digit that only `SELECT aurora_version();` shows, and it arrives as this pending action. No code change is needed and none causes drift. (Aurora MySQL 2 and 3 differ: their version string includes the patch level, so a patch there changes the engine version.)
The pending action carries no CVE list. A CVE is named here only when an AWS bulletin ties it to this engine and the patch's version.

With zero-downtime patching (Aurora PostgreSQL 10.21, 11.16, 12.11, 13.7, 14.3, 15.3, 16.1 and higher) the writer keeps most connections: a drop in throughput that typically lasts a few seconds, at most about one minute. Connections are still dropped when long-running queries or transactions, DDL, temporary tables or table locks, sessions listening on notification channels, `WITH HOLD` cursors or TLSv1.1 are in use. Zero-downtime patching does not cover reader instances: they restart. Without it the database is shut down and every connection and transaction in progress is lost.

An action with an apply date is applied by AWS in the cluster's maintenance window after that date. With auto minor version upgrade on, Aurora also applies patches on its own schedule. An action without a date waits until someone applies it.

The person running this needs `rds:DescribePendingMaintenanceActions`, `rds:ApplyPendingMaintenanceAction`, `rds:DescribeDBClusters`, `rds:DescribeEvents` and `rds:CreateDBClusterSnapshot` on this cluster, and a database login to run `SELECT aurora_version();`.
Confirm the patch is still pending and read its description and dates.
Pick a low-traffic period, and clear parameter changes that are in a `pending` state first: they interfere with zero-downtime patching. Clients should retry with exponential backoff and jitter.

If the cluster is in an Aurora global database, apply pending maintenance on the secondary clusters before the primary. Managed cross-Region switchover and failover have patch level requirements across the member clusters.
Aurora takes its own pre-upgrade snapshot for major version upgrades only, not for minor versions or patches. Take a manual cluster snapshot first.
RDS console, Region {region} > Databases > select the cluster `{cluster}` > Actions > Patch at next window (or Patch now).
Schedule the patch for the cluster's next maintenance window.
Or apply it now, in a quiet period. An immediate opt-in can't be undone.

The engine version string stays the same; the patch shows in `SELECT aurora_version();` (three numbers). The action leaves the pending list (eventually consistent: poll with backoff for up to five minutes). Check the cluster is `available` and the application reconnected.

A scheduled patch that has not started can be cancelled with `undo-opt-in`; an immediate opt-in can't be undone. AWS documents no way back from an applied patch, and Aurora PostgreSQL does not support restoring a snapshot, or a point in time, to a previous minor version.
An engine version upgrade of the cluster (`db-upgrade`, or a new minor version). It has a code equivalent: the cluster's engine version.
This has a code equivalent: the engine version of the cluster resource. Applying it in AWS instead leaves a version pinned in code behind the live one.
The pending action carries no CVE list. A CVE is named here only when an AWS bulletin ties it to this engine and target version. For Aurora MySQL, AWS publishes which version first fixed each CVE.

Change `engine_version` on the `aws_rds_cluster` (or the module input or variable that feeds it). Never raise it on an `aws_rds_cluster_instance`: the provider says an upgrade must be done on the cluster and trying it on the instance will not update the version. A major version jump also needs `allow_major_version_upgrade = true`, and `db_cluster_parameter_group_name` and `db_instance_parameter_group_name` of the new family. A member of an `aws_rds_global_cluster` is upgraded through the global cluster, with `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [engine_version] }` on the member.

`apply_immediately` defaults to `false`: after apply the upgrade is queued for the cluster's next maintenance window and the plan keeps showing a difference until it runs. With `apply_immediately = true` the outage happens at apply time. The provider notes that updating `engine_version` results in an outage.

`engine_version` updates in place. The provider documents these as forcing a new cluster: `cluster_identifier`, `cluster_identifier_prefix`, `cluster_scalability_type`, `publicly_accessible`, `availability_zones`; and on a cluster instance: `availability_zone`, `cluster_identifier`, `db_subnet_group_name`, `engine`, `identifier`, `identifier_prefix`. CoderHelm also refuses a change to `snapshot_identifier` or `global_cluster_identifier` in an upgrade change.

Never set a value below the live version: a pinned version behind the live one makes the next apply a downgrade attempt, which RDS refuses. Aurora MySQL 2 and 3 version strings include the patch level (`8.0.mysql_aurora.3.08.2`), so a fully pinned value falls behind whenever AWS patches; Aurora PostgreSQL values are major.minor, so only minor versions move. The running version is `engine_version_actual`.

Change `EngineVersion` on the `AWS::RDS::DBCluster` (Update requires: Some interruptions; in place). Not on a member `AWS::RDS::DBInstance`: for Aurora the property is not applicable there, the cluster manages it. If the cluster is a member of a global database, do not use this property: set `EngineVersion` on the `AWS::RDS::GlobalCluster`.

CloudFormation cannot schedule cluster modifications for the maintenance window: the upgrade starts when the stack update runs. To upgrade in the maintenance window instead, AWS says to use `modify-db-cluster` or the console, and then the template must be raised to match.

`EngineVersion` is not a replacement property. `DBClusterIdentifier`, `SnapshotIdentifier` and `EngineMode` are (removing `SnapshotIdentifier` from a cluster that was restored from one creates an empty cluster and deletes the original). Changing the logical id of the resource replaces it too. The default `DeletionPolicy` of a DB cluster is `Snapshot`.

CloudFormation compares templates, not live values. For Aurora MySQL the version string changes when AWS patches the cluster, and AWS warns that this change in `EngineVersion` can trigger actions by CloudFormation. Set the template to at least the live version; never below it.

Change the engine version on the cluster's `engine` (for example `rds.AuroraPostgresEngineVersion.VER_16_1` or `rds.AuroraMysqlEngineVersion.VER_3_07_0`; use the class's static `of(...)` when the library has no constant for the target). CDK passes it to the cluster's `EngineVersion`, an in-place update.

The upgrade starts when the stack deploys: CloudFormation does not support scheduling cluster modifications for the maintenance window. The default instance update behaviour is BULK, where all instances might be unavailable at the same time; `instanceUpdateBehaviour: rds.InstanceUpdateBehaviour.ROLLING` updates one instance at a time.
Changing a construct id changes the logical id, and CloudFormation then replaces the resource. Keep every construct id and the cluster identifier as they are. The default `removalPolicy` is SNAPSHOT.

A minor version upgrade restarts the cluster. Aurora PostgreSQL with zero-downtime patching keeps most writer connections (a drop in throughput of a few seconds to about one minute) and restarts the readers; without it every connection is lost. Aurora MySQL zero-downtime patching is best effort and the length of the outage varies with workload, cluster size and binary log data. Zero-downtime patching does not apply to major version upgrades: after the writer is upgraded each reader has a brief outage.
The person running this needs `rds:DescribeDBEngineVersions`, `rds:DescribeDBClusters`, `rds:CreateDBClusterSnapshot`, `rds:ModifyDBCluster` and `rds:DescribeEvents` on this cluster.
Confirm the target is a valid upgrade from the running version.

The cluster must be `available`. Clear pending parameter changes (they interfere with zero-downtime patching). If the cluster is in a global database, upgrade the secondary clusters before the primary, or upgrade the global cluster.
Test the upgrade on a copy first: restore a recent snapshot or clone the cluster, upgrade the copy and run the application's tests. New minor versions can change query plans.

For a major upgrade of Aurora PostgreSQL: prepare a DB cluster parameter group and a DB parameter group for the new version; no open prepared transactions; logical replication slots block the upgrade on source versions before 17; update extensions such as PostGIS and pgRouting first.
Take a manual cluster snapshot before the upgrade. Aurora takes its own pre-upgrade snapshot for major version upgrades only, not for minor versions.

RDS console, Region {region} > Databases > select the cluster `{cluster}` > Modify > DB engine version: {target} > Continue > choose Apply during the next scheduled maintenance window (or Apply immediately) > Modify cluster.
Upgrade the cluster in its next maintenance window. Add `--allow-major-version-upgrade` for a major version jump; use `--apply-immediately` to upgrade now.
The cluster is `available` again and its engine version is the target; `SELECT aurora_version();` shows the full version. Check the application reconnected and watch for query plan regressions.

Upgrades are one-way. Aurora PostgreSQL does not support restoring a snapshot, or a point in time, to a previous minor version, so there is no way back from a minor upgrade; test on a clone first. After a major upgrade the pre-upgrade snapshot can restore the previous version into a new cluster. Reverting the version in code is not a rollback: it asks for a downgrade. Aurora rolls back by itself only when a major upgrade fails.

Aurora minor versions are available for at least 12 months. After that Aurora may upgrade the cluster to the default minor version in a maintenance window even when auto minor version upgrade is off, with a reminder and cluster event `RDS-EVENT-0156` beforehand. Aurora global databases do not get automatic minor version upgrades.
